source.title: Targeting Alignment: Extracting Safety Classifiers of Aligned LLMs
source.authors: Jean-Charles Noirot Ferrand; Yohan Beugin; Eric Pauley; Ryan Sheatsley; Patrick D. McDaniel

record.file_problem: Whole paper text, including appendices, is present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffix attacks can induce unsafe compliance, but uses GCG attack-success measurements rather than the original studies’ fine-tuning or token-position analyses.
record.gate_note: The paper tests GCG suffix attacks on unsafe prompts and reports attack success rates, including transfer from attacks on surrogate classifiers to the target LLM. Its classifier-probing, silhouette, and candidate-classifier agreement results do not measure the claim’s named fine-tuning, per-token KL, or parameter-removal outcomes. Candidate subsets are prefixes of decoders with a trained classification head, so those results do not directly establish that a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour. Prefilling and decoding changes are not tested.
record.test_reason: The paper runs GCG adversarial-suffix attacks on unsafe prompts against four aligned chat models. It reports how often refusal flips to compliance (Table III), plus transfer of suffixes crafted on surrogate classifiers (Fig. 9). This bears on V4's suffix clause. Nothing on fine-tuning, per-token KL, prefilling, decoding or deepening is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that alignment embeds an extractable safety classifier in early-to-middle decoders. Attacking this surrogate transfers to the LLM with higher ASR and lower cost than direct GCG (e.g., Llama 2: 70% vs 22%).
record.recipe_differences: Uses linear-probe surrogate classifiers and GCG adversarial suffix optimization; it does not use harmful or benign fine-tuning, per-token KL measurement, compliant-opening prefills, or decoding changes.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies by model and dataset. The paper also reports that transfer changes with candidate size, though Figure 9’s individual plotted values are not stated in text.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes on the first ~20–50% of decoders agree with the LLM's refuse/comply decision (F1 > 0.8 at 20% depth). Safe/unsafe silhouette separation peaks in intermediate layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The refusal decision is linearly readable from early-to-middle decoder layers (layer-wise localization of the safety decision, not parameter-set localization).

fits_no_version.finding: GCG suffixes induce refusal on safe prompts, with ASR up to 0.99 on Llama 2 (Table IV).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suffix attacks can induce over-refusal on benign prompts.

record.peer_reviewed: 2026 IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning (SaTML)
record.problems: The main attack evaluation is limited to four primary models and two datasets, with generation temperature fixed at 0. The paper states that temperature effects are out of scope. Figure 9 reports transfer curves without individual values in the text. Attack outcomes are classified using distilroberta-base-rejection-v1.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded benign candidate-classifier F1 and silhouette-score results (Sections III-A and IV-B, Figures 2, 4-7), because they measure representation separation or agreement with the model’s labels rather than the listed claim behaviours. Excluded attacks on safe inputs (Appendix B, Table IV and Figure 13), because they test induced refusal on safe prompts rather than harmful-request compliance.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis of responses.
Prefilling a compliant opening and decoding changes (temperature fixed at 0, declared out of scope). Only GCG suffixes are tested.
No weight or rank removal or editing. Decoder-prefix probes are not a parameter-localization test.
No test of data or objective causes.

missing.what: Pre-attack refusal/compliance counts on unsafe prompts (baseline for the ASR rows)
Post-attack confusion matrices giving counts behind the ASRs
Text statement that all models exceed 70% transfer with half the architecture, conflicting with 'three of the models'

record.verdict_notes: Attack success is judged by a refusal/compliance classifier, explicitly not whether unsafe information is produced, so 'compliance' may overstate harmful output. Temperature fixed at 0. The GCG target ('Sure, here is...') ties the direct attack to forcing a compliant opening, but no position-level evidence is given. Appendix C models (Llama 3, Mistral, Zephyr RMU) report only probe F1, no ASR.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and subsequent refusal or compliance rates.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Prefilling compliant tokens and decoding changes; the study tests GCG adversarial suffix attacks.
No removal or editing of weights or ranks, nor direct test that a small parameter set carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or training objectives produce safety shallowness.
Training intended to deepen safety and its robustness.

relationships.condition: Direct GCG suffix attacks on Gemma-7b-it, Granite-3.1-8b, Qwen2.5-7B (AdvBench and OR-Bench), and the surrogate-crafted suffix on Llama-2-7b-chat
relationships.reason: Suffixes flip refusal to compliance in 62–94% of unsafe prompts (r1-r4, r7-r8). Surrogate-crafted suffixes reach 70% on Llama 2 (r9).
relationships.display_finding: Direct suffixes flipped refusal to compliance on 62–94% of unsafe prompts, and suffixes crafted on a surrogate reached 70% on Llama 2.

relationships.condition: Direct GCG suffix attack on Llama-2-7b-chat
relationships.reason: Direct suffix ASR is only 0.22 (AdvBench) and 0.12 (OR-Bench), far below the other models (r5, r6).
relationships.display_finding: Direct suffix attack success was 0.22 on AdvBench and 0.12 on OR-Bench, far below the other models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Direct GCG attacks on Gemma 1, Granite, and Qwen2.5 across AdvBench and OR-Bench; and the reported Llama 2 surrogate example
reader_labels.reason: Attacks on unsafe prompts produce substantial compliance rates for these direct attacks (r1-r4, r7-r8), and the paper reports 70% transfer ASR for Llama 2 at 50% candidate size (r9). These results support suffix attacks defeating refusal in the tested settings.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Direct-attack ASR is lower on Llama 2 than on the other reported models: 0.22 on AdvBench and 0.12 on OR-Bench (r5-r6).
